outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Factual Setting, Claims, and Appellate Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the dispute arising from Jimmy Kimmel’s use of fictitious identities to purchase George Santos Cameo videos and then air them on Jimmy Kimmel Live! as part of a comedic segment. It explains the claims Santos brought, the district court’s Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal, and the standards governing appellate review and the materials the Second Circuit could consider at the pleading stage.
subtopics: The Cameo transactions: Santos creates personalized videos in response to requests submitted under false names
The challenged use: Kimmel airs the videos in the recurring segment 'Will Santos Say It?'
The defendants: Kimmel, ABC, Jimmy Kimmel Live!, and Disney
Santos’s causes of action: copyright infringement and related state law claims
The district court’s disposition: dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6)
The issues on appeal: fair use, preemption, contract theories, and fraudulent inducement
Standard of review on appeal: de novo review of a motion-to-dismiss ruling
What the court may consider on a Rule 12(b)(6) appeal: complaint allegations, incorporated documents, exhibits, and judicially noticed copyright registrations

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Fair Use Framework and the Court’s Treatment of Transformative Purpose
outline.description: This chapter explains the court’s fair use framework and why the first factor—purpose and character of the use—dominated the analysis. It focuses on the court’s conclusion that Kimmel’s use was transformative because the broadcast segments repurposed the Cameo videos for criticism and commentary about Santos’s willingness to say absurd things for money.
subtopics: Fair use as an affirmative defense that can justify otherwise infringing conduct
The four statutory fair use factors under 17 U.S.C. § 107
Why fair use may be resolved at the pleading stage when established on the face of the complaint
The centrality of transformative use in the first-factor analysis
The governing inquiry after Warhol: objective purpose rather than subjective intent
Santos’s argument that Kimmel 'instigated' the original works and therefore shared their original purpose
The court’s rejection of Santos’s subjective-purpose theory
Reasonable observer analysis: original Cameo videos as conveying positivity, encouragement, and hope
Kimmel’s new purpose: sarcastic criticism and commentary in a late-night comedy segment
Why the first factor strongly favored fair use

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: The Remaining Fair Use Factors and Why Copyright Claims Failed at the Pleading Stage
outline.description: This chapter covers the court’s analysis of Santos’s other fair use arguments, including bad faith, publication, amount used, and market harm. It shows how the court concluded that no further factual development was needed because comparing the original videos and the aired segments was sufficient to establish fair use on the pleadings.
subtopics: Santos’s bad-faith argument based on Kimmel’s use of false identities
The court’s treatment of Harper & Row’s 'good faith and fair dealing' language
Why alleged deception did not defeat fair use where the use was for criticism rather than market substitution
The second factor: the nature of the copyrighted works
The significance of the copyright registrations showing same-day publication
The third factor: the amount and substantiality of the use in the context of commentary and criticism
The fourth factor: market harm and the distinction between criticism that devalues a work and substitution that usurps its market
Why parody, lampooning, or critical commentary ordinarily does not invade a cognizable licensing market
The court’s reliance on the complaint itself to find no plausible market usurpation
The conclusion that fair use barred the copyright claims even on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: The State Law Contract Claims—Third-Party Beneficiary and Implied-in-Fact Theories
outline.description: This chapter explains why the court affirmed dismissal of Santos’s contract-based claims without resolving copyright preemption. It separates the direct breach claim under Cameo’s Terms of Service from the implied contract theory and shows how choice-of-law rules and pleading deficiencies independently defeated both claims.
subtopics: The district court’s preemption ruling and the Second Circuit’s decision to bypass the preemption issue
Why a court may affirm on state-law failure-to-state-a-claim grounds instead of reaching preemption
The direct breach of contract theory based on Cameo’s Terms of Service
Illinois law governing the Terms of Service
The strong presumption against third-party beneficiary status under Illinois law
The requirement that third-party benefit be practically an express declaration
Why Santos was not a party to the Terms of Service and could not enforce them
The significance of other Terms of Service provisions that expressly mention third-party beneficiaries
The implied-in-fact contract claim under New York law
Requirements for pleading formation and essential terms of an implied contract
The complaint’s failure to allege nonconclusory essential terms
The absence of a plausible meeting of the minds that Kimmel would be bound to the Terms of Service as between Kimmel and Santos

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: Fraudulent Inducement, Disposition, and the Opinion’s Practical Significance
outline.description: This final chapter addresses the fraudulent inducement claim and then synthesizes the court’s overall disposition. It highlights the opinion’s practical lessons about pleading fair use, the limits of state-law claims built around copyrighted works, and the distinction between reputational harm and legally cognizable economic loss.
subtopics: Santos’s fraudulent inducement theory based on misrepresentations used to obtain the videos
New York’s out-of-pocket loss rule for fraud damages
Why Santos failed to plead actual pecuniary loss caused by the alleged fraud
The court’s affirmance of dismissal of the fraudulent inducement claim
The final disposition: affirmance of the district court’s judgment in full
How the opinion ties together copyright fair use and state-law pleading rules
The significance of the case for expressive reuse in comedy, criticism, and commentary
The case’s lesson on pleading-stage fair use in the Second Circuit
The difference between injury to dignity or reputation and compensable market or out-of-pocket loss
